claim: Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive (MS) ion channel with characteristic fast-inactivation kinetics.
source: Piezo1 is a mechanosensitive (MS) ion channel with characteristic fast-inactivation kinetics.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Piezo1 channels, referenced in the introduction.

claim: A slowly-inactivating MS current was found in mouse embryonic stem (mES) cells.
source: We found a slowly-inactivating MS current in mouse embryonic stem (mES) cells and characterized it throughout their differentiation into motor-neurons to investigate its components.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: MS currents in mES cells were large and slowly-inactivating in the stem-cell stage.
source: MS currents were large and slowly-inactivating in the stem-cell stage, and became smaller and faster-inactivating throughout the differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: MS currents became smaller and faster-inactivating throughout differentiation of mES cells into motor neurons.
source: MS currents were large and slowly-inactivating in the stem-cell stage, and became smaller and faster-inactivating throughout the differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in mES cells.
source: We found that Piezo1 is expressed in mES cells, and its knockout abolishes MS currents, indicating that the slowly-inactivating current in mES cells is carried by Piezo1.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 5B and knockout experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Knockout of Piezo1 abolishes MS currents in mES cells.
source: We found that Piezo1 is expressed in mES cells, and its knockout abolishes MS currents, indicating that the slowly-inactivating current in mES cells is carried by Piezo1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The slowly-inactivating current in mES cells is carried by Piezo1.
source: We found that Piezo1 is expressed in mES cells, and its knockout abolishes MS currents, indicating that the slowly-inactivating current in mES cells is carried by Piezo1.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of expression data and knockout experiments showing complete loss of MS currents.

claim: Piezo1 cDNA from mES cells displays fast-inactivation kinetics in heterologous expression.
source: To further investigate its slow inactivation in these cells, we cloned Piezo1 cDNA from mES cells and found that it displays fast-inactivation kinetics in heterologous expression, indicating that sources of modulation other than the aminoacid sequence determine its slow kinetics in mES cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Sources of modulation other than the amino acid sequence determine the slow kinetics of Piezo1 in mES cells.
source: To further investigate its slow inactivation in these cells, we cloned Piezo1 cDNA from mES cells and found that it displays fast-inactivation kinetics in heterologous expression, indicating that sources of modulation other than the aminoacid sequence determine its slow kinetics in mES cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the same sequence shows different kinetics in different cellular contexts.

claim: Piezo1 knockout ES cells showed a reduced rate of proliferation.
source: Finally, we report that Piezo1 knockout ES cells showed a reduced rate of proliferation but no significant differences in other markers of pluripotency and differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Piezo1 knockout ES cells showed no significant differences in markers of pluripotency and differentiation.
source: Finally, we report that Piezo1 knockout ES cells showed a reduced rate of proliferation but no significant differences in other markers of pluripotency and differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: Piezos are present in most eukaryotes with the notable exception of yeasts.
source: Piezos are present in most eukaryotes (with the notable exception of yeasts) (Xiao and Xu, 2010) where they mediate light-touch sensation (Ranade et al., 2014b), vascular endothelial development (Li et al., 2014), and respiratory control (Nonomura et al., 2017), to name just a few.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xiao and Xu, 2010.

claim: Piezos mediate light-touch sensation.
source: Piezos are present in most eukaryotes (with the notable exception of yeasts) (Xiao and Xu, 2010) where they mediate light-touch sensation (Ranade et al., 2014b), vascular endothelial development (Li et al., 2014), and respiratory control (Nonomura et al., 2017), to name just a few.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ranade et al., 2014b.

claim: Piezos mediate vascular endothelial development.
source: Piezos are present in most eukaryotes (with the notable exception of yeasts) (Xiao and Xu, 2010) where they mediate light-touch sensation (Ranade et al., 2014b), vascular endothelial development (Li et al., 2014), and respiratory control (Nonomura et al., 2017), to name just a few.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Piezos mediate respiratory control.
source: Piezos are present in most eukaryotes (with the notable exception of yeasts) (Xiao and Xu, 2010) where they mediate light-touch sensation (Ranade et al., 2014b), vascular endothelial development (Li et al., 2014), and respiratory control (Nonomura et al., 2017), to name just a few.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nonomura et al., 2017.

claim: In their canonical forms, Piezos inactivate quickly following stimulation with a time constant less than 20 ms.
source: Though modest variations have been reported (Schneider et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2014; Ikeda et al., 2014), in their canonical forms, they inactivate quickly following stimulation with a time constant less than 20 ms and in a voltage-dependent manner (Coste et al., 2010; 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coste et al., 2010 and 2012.

claim: Piezos inactivate in a voltage-dependent manner.
source: Though modest variations have been reported (Schneider et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2014; Ikeda et al., 2014), in their canonical forms, they inactivate quickly following stimulation with a time constant less than 20 ms and in a voltage-dependent manner (Coste et al., 2010; 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coste et al., 2010 and 2012.

claim: Loss of function by knockout of either member of the Piezo family is either unviable or severely debilitating in mammals.
source: In mammals, loss of function by knockout of either member of the Piezo family is either unviable (Ranade et al., 2014b; 2014a), or severely debilitating (Chesler et al., 2016; Delle Vedove et al., 2016; Haliloglu et al., 2017) but gain of function mutations can also result in severe defects: mutations in the human PIEZO1 gene that cause slow inactivation have recently been associated with hereditary xerocytosis, a disorder of ionic imbalance in red blood cells (Albuisson et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Ranade et al., 2014a and 2014b, Chesler et al., 2016, Delle Vedove et al., 2016, and Haliloglu et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations in the human PIEZO1 gene that cause slow inactivation have been associated with hereditary xerocytosis.
source: In mammals, loss of function by knockout of either member of the Piezo family is either unviable (Ranade et al., 2014b; 2014a), or severely debilitating (Chesler et al., 2016; Delle Vedove et al., 2016; Haliloglu et al., 2017) but gain of function mutations can also result in severe defects: mutations in the human PIEZO1 gene that cause slow inactivation have recently been associated with hereditary xerocytosis, a disorder of ionic imbalance in red blood cells (Albuisson et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Albuisson et al., 2013 and Bae et al., 2013.

claim: Hereditary xerocytosis is a disorder of ionic imbalance in red blood cells.
source: In mammals, loss of function by knockout of either member of the Piezo family is either unviable (Ranade et al., 2014b; 2014a), or severely debilitating (Chesler et al., 2016; Delle Vedove et al., 2016; Haliloglu et al., 2017) but gain of function mutations can also result in severe defects: mutations in the human PIEZO1 gene that cause slow inactivation have recently been associated with hereditary xerocytosis, a disorder of ionic imbalance in red blood cells (Albuisson et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about hereditary xerocytosis.

claim: Dorsal root ganglia cells display three types of mechanosensory ionic currents when directly stimulated with a probe: rapid-, intermediate-, and slow-inactivating currents.
source: For example, dorsal root ganglia cells display three types of mechanosensory ionic currents when directly stimulated with a probe: rapid-, intermediate-, and slow-inactivating currents (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2010.

claim: Piezo2 only accounts for the rapid-inactivating responses in dorsal root ganglia cells.
source: Piezo2 only accounts for the rapid-inactivating responses, with slow- and non-inactivating conductances still uncharacterized.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2010 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Slow- and non-inactivating conductances in dorsal root ganglia cells are still uncharacterized.
source: Piezo2 only accounts for the rapid-inactivating responses, with slow- and non-inactivating conductances still uncharacterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: C2C12 cells express a form of slow-inactivating mechanosensory current that is not yet characterized.
source: Other cultured cell lines like C2C12 also express a form of slow-inactivating mechanosensory current, also not yet characterized (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2010.

claim: The cellular fate of multipotent stem cells can be influenced by mechanical strain, shear stress, substrate stiffness or elasticity.
source: Multiple reports show that the cellular fate of multipotent stem cells can be influenced by mechanical strain, shear stress, substrate stiffness or elasticity (Blumenthal et al., 2014; Engler et al., 2006; Ivanovska et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2016; Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Blumenthal et al., 2014, Engler et al., 2006, Ivanovska et al., 2015, Lu et al., 2016, and Pathak et al., 2014.

claim: MS currents in mES cells ranged from 0 to over 2100 pA over baseline, with an average value of 465 ± 112 pA (n = 30).
source: Currents ranged from 0 to over 2100 pA over baseline, with an average value of 465 ± 112 pA (n = 30).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: The slow fraction of MS current in mES cells had an average value of 0.67 ± 0.04 (n = 30).
source: In mES cells the slow fraction of MS current had an average value 0.67 ± 0.04 (n = 30) and in some cells it approached 1.0.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claim: For a canonical fast-inactivating channel such as Piezo1, the slow fraction is typically less than 0.2.
source: For a canonical fast-inactivating channel such as Piezo1 the slow fraction is typically less than 0.2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Piezo1 channel behavior.

claim: The MS currents in mES cells have a permeability sequence of PCa > PK = PNa> PNMDG.
source: A detailed study of the MS currents in mES cells revealed that they are selective for cations with a permeability sequence as defined by the reversal potential under bi-ionic conditions: PCa > PK = PNa> PNMDG (Figure 1B) (Hille, 1992, pg 19).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and referenced to Hille, 1992.

claim: The MS currents in mES cells are selective for cations.
source: A detailed study of the MS currents in mES cells revealed that they are selective for cations with a permeability sequence as defined by the reversal potential under bi-ionic conditions: PCa > PK = PNa> PNMDG (Figure 1B) (Hille, 1992, pg 19).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In excised membrane patches, stimulation by pressure clamp elicited single mechanosensitive channels that correlated temporally with stimulation.
source: In excised membrane patches, stimulation by pressure clamp elicited single mechanosensitive channels that correlated temporally with stimulation (Figure 2 label panels A, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2D.

claim: An ensemble of multiple pressure-evoked recordings of single channels at the same voltage yielded macroscopic currents whose kinetics mimic the whole cell MS currents activated by poking.
source: An ensemble of multiple pressure-evoked recordings of single channels at the same voltage yielded macroscopic currents whose kinetics mimic the whole cell MS currents activated by poking (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The single channel conductance of MS channels in mES cells is 24.7 ± 2.5 pS in standard physiological conditions.
source: Amplitude histograms at multiple voltages revealed a single channel conductance of 24.7 ± 2.5 pS in standard physiological conditions (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Voltage-dependent currents in mES cells were small and remained so throughout the first 4 days of differentiation until neuronal stages were approached.
source: Voltage-dependent currents in mES cells were small and remained so throughout the first 4 days until neuronal stages were approached.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Around day five of differentiation, voltage-dependent potassium currents became larger and some cells began to exhibit small voltage-dependent sodium currents.
source: Around day five voltage-dependent potassium currents became larger and some cells began to exhibit small voltage-dependent sodium currents (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: By day 7 of differentiation, GFP expression increased and GFP-positive cells acquired a typical neuronal profile of large voltage-dependent K+ and Na+ currents and were able to fire action potentials.
source: By day 7, GFP expression increased and GFP-positive cells acquired a typical neuronal profile of large voltage-dependent K+ and Na+ currents and were able to fire action potentials.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The expression of Piezo1 throughout the differentiation correlates with the fast component of the mechanosensitive current.
source: The expression of Piezo1 throughout the differentiation strikingly resembles the evolution of the fast component of the mechanosensitive current.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Two independent Piezo1 knockout clones of mouse embryonic stem cells showed no mechanosensitive activity.
source: Both Piezo1 knock-out colonies of mouse embryonic stem cells showed no mechanosensitive activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The cDNA recovered from mES cells encodes a Piezo1 protein that contains three amino acid substitutions compared to the original sequence cloned from N2A cells: G147R, I229V, and V1572M.
source: The cDNA recovered from mES cells encodes a protein that contains three amino acid substitutions compared to the original sequence cloned from N2A cells: G147R, I229V, and V1572M.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of cloned cDNA.

claim: Both Piezo1 constructs from N2A and mES cells yielded currents with similar, fast inactivation kinetics when expressed in HEK 293 cells.
source: Both constructs yielded currents with similar, fast inactivation kinetics (Figure 6A,B), excluding the point substitutions as accounting for the altered kinetics of Piezo1 in mES cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The point substitutions in Piezo1 from mES cells do not account for the altered kinetics of Piezo1 in mES cells.
source: Both constructs yielded currents with similar, fast inactivation kinetics (Figure 6A,B), excluding the point substitutions as accounting for the altered kinetics of Piezo1 in mES cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both constructs show similar kinetics in heterologous expression.

claim: During naïve inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in the organization of mESC colonies between Piezo1 knockout and wild type lines.
source: During 'naïve' inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in the organization of mESC colonies, expression of pluripotency transcription factors (SOX2), typical cell-to-cell or cell-to-substrate adhesions (E-Cadherin, F-Actin), or size of colonies (Figure 7A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: During naïve inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in expression of pluripotency transcription factors (SOX2) between Piezo1 knockout and wild type lines.
source: During 'naïve' inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in the organization of mESC colonies, expression of pluripotency transcription factors (SOX2), typical cell-to-cell or cell-to-substrate adhesions (E-Cadherin, F-Actin), or size of colonies (Figure 7A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: During naïve inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in typical cell-to-cell or cell-to-substrate adhesions (E-Cadherin, F-Actin) between Piezo1 knockout and wild type lines.
source: During 'naïve' inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in the organization of mESC colonies, expression of pluripotency transcription factors (SOX2), typical cell-to-cell or cell-to-substrate adhesions (E-Cadherin, F-Actin), or size of colonies (Figure 7A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: During naïve inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in size of colonies between Piezo1 knockout and wild type lines.
source: During 'naïve' inner cell mass pluripotency (mESC) there was no significant difference in the organization of mESC colonies, expression of pluripotency transcription factors (SOX2), typical cell-to-cell or cell-to-substrate adhesions (E-Cadherin, F-Actin), or size of colonies (Figure 7A, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Table 1.

claim: Overall proliferation rates were significantly lower in Piezo1 knockout compared to wild type genotypes.
source: Overall proliferation rates however, were significantly lower in KO compared to WT genotypes, suggesting Piezo1 supports normal proliferation at this stage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Piezo1 supports normal proliferation at the mESC stage.
source: Overall proliferation rates however, were significantly lower in KO compared to WT genotypes, suggesting Piezo1 supports normal proliferation at this stage (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockout cells have reduced proliferation.

claim: There was no significant difference in the percentage of cells in M-phase (PH-H3) between Piezo1 knockout and wild type genotypes.
source: There was no significant difference in the percentage of cells in M-phase (PH-H3), and negligible evidence for cell death in either genotype (activated caspase three or pyknotic nuclei < 0.1%) (Figure 1C, Table 1), we therefore concluded the decreased proliferation was likely due to lengthening of cell cycle interphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Table 1.

claim: There was negligible evidence for cell death in either Piezo1 knockout or wild type genotype (activated caspase three or pyknotic nuclei < 0.1%).
source: There was no significant difference in the percentage of cells in M-phase (PH-H3), and negligible evidence for cell death in either genotype (activated caspase three or pyknotic nuclei < 0.1%) (Figure 1C, Table 1), we therefore concluded the decreased proliferation was likely due to lengthening of cell cycle interphase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Table 1.

claim: The decreased proliferation in Piezo1 knockout cells was likely due to lengthening of cell cycle interphase.
source: There was no significant difference in the percentage of cells in M-phase (PH-H3), and negligible evidence for cell death in either genotype (activated caspase three or pyknotic nuclei < 0.1%) (Figure 1C, Table 1), we therefore concluded the decreased proliferation was likely due to lengthening of cell cycle interphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that M-phase percentage and cell death are similar between genotypes.

claim: There was no significant difference between WT and Piezo1 knockout clones in marker expression at naïve (mESC), primed (EpiSC) and gastrulation stage differentiation.
source: Quantitative cell scoring showed no significant difference between WT (n = 2) and PZ1KO (n = 3) clones, mean% of cells/line+/sd at each stage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and Table 1.

claim: Wild type mESC showed a lower rate of spontaneous differentiation when cultured on a soft (28 kPa, PDMS) substrate compared to standard tissue culture plastic (100,000 kPa).
source: Wild type mESC showed a lower rate of spontaneous differentiation under pluripotency conditions when cultured on a soft (28 kPa, PDMS) substrate compared to standard tissue culture plastic (100,000 kPa) following previous reports (Chowdhury et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and citation to Chowdhury et al., 2010.

claim: Piezo1 knockout clones showed the same differential differentiation inhibiting response to substrate stiffness as wild type cells.
source: Piezo1 knockout clones showed the same relationship, indicating no effect of Piezo1 in mediating this response to substrate stiffness (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Piezo1 does not affect the response to substrate stiffness in mESC.
source: Piezo1 knockout clones showed the same relationship, indicating no effect of Piezo1 in mediating this response to substrate stiffness (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that knockout and wild type cells show similar responses to substrate stiffness.

claim: While Piezo1 is expressed during pluripotency and mediates normal proliferation rate, it does not grossly affect the pluripotency per se, early germ layer differentiation, or response to substrate stiffness.
source: We conclude that while Piezo1 is expressed during pluripotency and mediates normal proliferation rate, it does not grossly affect the pluripotency per se, early germ layer differentiation, or response to substrate stiffness.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental observations presented in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: The identity of the MS current in mES cells is unequivocally assigned to Piezo1.
source: The identity of this MS current is therefore unequivocally assigned to Piezo1.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of single channel properties, ion selectivity, and knockout experiments.

claim: Mechanical properties of the growth substrate can modulate the lineage choice of neural stem cells.
source: For example, mechanical properties of the growth substrate can modulate the lineage choice of neural stem cells (Pathak et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pathak et al., 2014.

claim: Mesenchymal stem cells have long been known to be influenced by matrix elasticity.
source: Other multipotent stem cells, like mesenchymal stem cells, have long been known to be influenced by matrix elasticity (Engler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Engler et al., 2006.

claim: The presence of mechanosensitive ion channels such as Piezo1 suggests a role for MS channels as potential transduction molecules in stem cells.
source: Although the action pathway of these variables is not fully understood, the presence of mechanosensitive ion channels such as Piezo1 suggests a role for MS channels as potential transduction molecules in stem cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the presence of Piezo1 in stem cells and known mechanical influences on stem cell fate.

claim: Regulation of Piezo1 kinetics can arise from either additional components (e.g. beta subunits) or from mechanical properties of the particular cellular environment, or a combination of both.
source: Regulation of its kinetics can arise from either additional components (e.g. beta subunits) or from mechanical properties of the particular cellular environment, or a combination of both.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms of Piezo1 regulation.

claim: There could exist additional components that shape the Piezo1 currents throughout the differentiation to modify their amplitude and kinetics into their final observed form.
source: In light of the results of this work, it is foreseeable that there could exist additional components that shape the Piezo1 currents throughout the differentiation to modify their amplitude and kinetics into their final observed form.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed changes in Piezo1 current properties during differentiation.

claim: The kinetics of human PIEZO1 can be regulated by pH.
source: In a recent work, Bae et al showed that the kinetics of human PIEZO1 can be regulated by pH (Bae et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bae et al., 2015.

claim: In certain conditions a fast inactivating Piezo1 channel can be 'converted' into a slow one by repeated stimulation.
source: Additionally, Sack's group observed that in certain conditions a fast inactivating Piezo1 channel can be 'converted' into a slow one by repeated stimulation (Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gottlieb et al., 2012.

claim: Stoml3 is required for mechanosensation in ~40% of myelinated mechanosensory fibers.
source: Stoml3, the mammalian counterpart of MEC-2, is required for mechanosensation in ~40% of myelinated mechanosensory fibers (Poole et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poole et al., 2014.

claim: Stoml3 tunes up the threshold of sensitivity of Piezo2 currents in DRGs, such that its absence increases the threshold of activation of Piezo2 by an order of magnitude.
source: This protein is reported to tune up the threshold of sensitivity of Piezo2 currents in DRGs, such that its absence increases the threshold of activation of Piezo2 by an order of magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poole et al., 2014 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Piezo1 currents can be increased and their thresholds lowered by expression of Stoml3.
source: The effect on Piezo2 is not specific: Piezo1 currents can too be increased and their thresholds lowered by expression of Stoml3.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poole et al., 2014 in the preceding sentences.

claim: Stoml3 protein co-precipitates with Piezo1 or Piezo2 after heterologous expression in HEK293 cells.
source: Additionally, Stoml3 protein co-precipitates with Piezo1 or Piezo2 after heterologous expression in HEK293 cells, indicating some degree of association.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Poole et al., 2014 in the preceding sentences.

claim: Polycystin-2 (PC2) is a proposed modulator of Piezo1 currents.
source: Polycystin-2 (PC2) is another proposed modulator of Piezo1 currents (Peyronnet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peyronnet et al., 2013.

claim: Overexpression of PC2 reduced endogenous Piezo1 currents in proximal convoluted tubule cells and in overexpression experiments in COS cells.
source: Overexpression of this protein reduced endogenous Piezo1 currents in proximal convoluted tubule cells and in overexpression experiments in COS cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peyronnet et al., 2013 in the preceding sentence.

claim: PC2 co-precipitates with Piezo1 when overexpressed in COS cells.
source: PC2 also co-precipitates with Piezo1 when overexpressed in COS cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peyronnet et al., 2013 in the preceding sentences.

claim: There is at least one novel source of slow- and/or intermediate- inactivating mechanosensitive currents present in DRGs.
source: Piezo1 is not supposedly expressed in those cells, so we are left to assume that there is still at least one novel source of slow- and/or intermediate- inactivating mechanosensitive currents present in DRGs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Piezo2 only accounts for fast-inactivating currents and Piezo1 is not expressed in DRGs.

claim: Overall Piezo1 KO ES cell lines showed minimal changes in pluripotency or differentiation in vitro compared to wild type lines.
source: Overall Piezo1 KO ES cell lines showed minimal changes in pluripotency or differentiation in vitro compared to wild type lines.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Table 1.

claim: Piezo1 KO mice show normal early development outside of the lethal ~e14 vascularization defect.
source: This finding fits with the normal early development reported for Piezo1 KO mice. However, outside of the lethal ~e14 vascularization defect reported for these mice, little specific or functional phenotyping was done, leaving open the possibility of subtle functional defects occurring early in development, which may be compensated by homeostatic developmental mechanisms.
evidence: This is based on previous reports about Piezo1 KO mice.

claim: The proliferation activity of Piezo1 could play a role in normal gastrulation by regulating the size of the epiblast.
source: The proliferation activity we identified could well play a role in normal gastrulation, by regulating the size of the epiblast, therefore influencing the functional geometry of the egg cylinder and ectoplacental cone, which triggers and organizes gastrulation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the potential role of Piezo1 in gastrulation.

claim: If Piezo1 plays a role in gastrulation, the viability of Piezo1 KO mice argues that this activity must be almost fully compensated for by an unknown homeostatic mechanism.
source: If so, the viability of Piezo1 KO mice argues that this activity must be almost fully compensated for by an unknown homeostatic mechanism, which could be identified in the future.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential compensation mechanisms.

claim: Hb9-GFP stem cells have a GFP transgene driven by the Hb9 promoter, a motor neuron specific promoter.
source: To monitor the differentiation we used Hb9-GFP stem cells, in which the motor neuron specific promoter Hb9 drives GFP expression (Wichterle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a description of the cell line used, supported by citation to Wichterle et al., 2002.

claim: Approximately 30% efficiency was achieved in motor neuron differentiation as assessed by GFP expression and morphological and functional characterization.
source: We achieved approximately 30% efficiency as assessed by GFP expression and morphological and functional characterization.
evidence: This is a quantitative assessment of the differentiation protocol.

claim: Three independent differentiations were performed, the same studies and measurements were carried out each time, and data from all three were combined.
source: Three independent differentiations were performed, the same studies and measurements were carried out each time, and data from all three were combined.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: No mechanically-evoked currents were present in differentiated motor neurons by day 7.
source: No mechanically-evoked currents were present by day 7.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 4.

claim: Two guide RNA sequences were used to generate a double strand break in the beginning of the first transmembrane region of Piezo1.
source: Two guide RNA sequences (sgRNAs) were chosen to generate a double strand break in the beginning of the first TM region.
evidence: This is a description of the CRISPR/Cas9 experimental design shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A two base-pair deletion generated a frame-shift mutation and an early stop codon in the Piezo1 knockout cells.
source: Below the diagram, a sequence reaction of a fragment of DNA extracted from one of the modified colonies is shown. In yellow is marked the targeted sgRNA sequence, and boxed in black is marked the region with a two base-pair deletion that generates a frame-shift mutation, and an early stop codon shortly after.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Only one sequence for each Piezo1 knockout colony was obtained after sequencing with no background, indicating a homozygous mutation.
source: Only one sequence for each colony was obtained after sequencing with no background, indicating a homozygous mutation.
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis of the knockout colonies.
